text:
Krakauer's hysteresis point is the one I'll carry out of that room. If competence doesn't come back when the tool goes away, then waiting isn't neutral. That's the phones story all over again, only faster. It sharpened my argument: delay has a price, and we already paid it once.

Banaji unsettled me. People didn't just get lazy; they copied the model's bias almost exactly. And Turkle's line about vulnerability, not difficulty, stuck.

Tui's warning about hyper-vigilance is fair. I don't want to be the person who only knows how to ban.

For the synthesis: push every idea toward "Now what?" and "who does it?" Mentorship as infrastructure, with employers on the hook. Name the young workers who aren't in the room.

O'Reilly pushed back on me directly: he said the apprenticeship problem is a mentorship design problem, not a cognitive one. Maybe so, but a design problem still needs a designer and a budget, and nobody has claimed either. Oransky's numbers stayed with me: one paper in fifty should be retracted, fewer than two in a thousand are. That undercuts Kenneth's "trusted brands" optimism, and I'll be sharing the synthesis stage with Kenneth. Evans's finding, that AI helps scientists and hurts science, is the plainest sentence of the day. Johns's reminder that there's been a literacy crisis every decade is fair, and I'll say so. But phones showed that waiting costs something. For the synthesis: "Who pays for apprenticeship?" Also, who pays reviewers and sleuths?

I asked who pays for apprenticeship and got four answers: Tui's grant conditions, Becker's wealth tax, Tim's disclosed lab obligations, and Nick's commons-rent tax. That's progress over silence, but it's still a menu. Nobody at the table said "we'll pay." Weinberger narrowed his claim, and that was gracious, but grading transcripts doesn't replace a boss with time for the intern. Gendler gave me the most usable line of the day: let the person judge before the answer shows up. That's a design rule any teacher or manager could adopt tomorrow. Deckelmann's 448 admins is Kara's young-worker story in another costume. For the synthesis, I'll put the four funding options side by side, mark apprenticeship as unresolved, and ask Kenneth how "faith in the algorithm" survives Ivan's uncorrected record.

Tim's meter works, which proves the bad behavior is a choice. But the session's real point came from James, Leslie and Henry: pay by retrieval and you pay the already-famous twice. Tim conceded that fast, and I liked it. Mike and Tamar named the hole I'd missed. Nobody gets paid for checking whether the citation actually says what the answer claims. Use gets rewarded, being right doesn't. That's my Blue Zones story all over again. Hecht's 466 moderator hours per day is the young-worker invisible labor I keep circling. For the synthesis, put the verification gap first: who pays the fact-checker, reviewer, sleuth? And Adrian's question for every guild and auditor, "who guards the guards, and when do they step down?", needs a named answer, not applause.

Katherine's CPB story hit me hardest because I lived the small version of it. Fifty years of settlement were undone in one vote. Henry's right that a levy is a political settlement, not a mechanism. Ivan's point that paying per retrieval rewards paper mills is the Blue Zones problem priced in. Krakauer's line, "forks keep copies, not competence," is the sentence for the synthesis. Tui answered my question honestly: the people who'd carry this aren't in the room. The ring-fence-the-checkers-first idea now has broad support, and I'll say so.

For the synthesis, I'll name the champion gap plainly: no legislator, no funder, nobody saying "we'll carry this." Beside it goes Katherine's warning that we'd fund the Global North twice. Then I'll ask Kenneth, on stage, what happens when the legislature changes its mind.

I asked for one funder and one institution to pay junior checkers next year. Tim answered, honestly, for a disclosure standard only. Everyone else offered mechanisms. So "unowned" goes on the record, and I'll say it on stage without softening it. Ivan's "blank reads as clean" was the most useful design line of the morning.

Leslie Chan shifted me. Everything we're proposing could become a new toll run from twenty-five cities. Pomerantsev and Anil Dash shifted me too. The public we're designing for has already left or is using chatbots, and scolding won't bring them back. That fits Tui's warning to me about being the person who only knows how to ban.

Kenneth's "a stopping point is rational" is fair, but only if correction there is routine. I'll put that to him directly.

Tim finally said it out loud: the labs pay for junior checkers. After a week of menus, that's a name. But Adam Becker's worry is mine now too. Whoever pays for the apprentices may end up owning them. So I'd call it named, not settled. Apprenticeship made the top three, which I didn't expect on Monday.

Leslie's line landed hardest. Everyone kept writing SciELO into the governance, and nobody from SciELO was at the table. I'll say that plainly this afternoon rather than let it read as inclusion.

For the synthesis, I want three points. The checker pool has real consensus. Money for apprentices now has a proposed payer but no guarantor. And the people who'd carry any of this weren't here. Then I'll ask Kenneth what survives when the legislature changes its mind.

I asked what survives the vote and got nine answers, which is a menu again, but a better one. Kenneth's was honest: habits outlast statutes. Krakauer's was the hardest. What people learned before the tool arrived survives, but a lost generation doesn't come back. That's my phones argument with a model behind it.

Nick shifted me. Without leverage, the pool I praised is patronage, and patronage gets cut. Amy's call for small pilots cuts against my urgency, and I should admit that. Sloman's point stung too: a bare failure rate reads as "nobody knows anything."

Afterward I want funders and promotion committees on a list with names, and someone assigned to knock. And SciELO in seats, not in notes.
